{\LARGE\bfseries\sffamily\color{AtlasNavy} Nonconvex second-order stationarity with complete high-order derivatives and independent tolerances\par}\vspace{5pt}
\textbf{Setting ID.} \texttt{SO\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}HO\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}HON05\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}S}

Single-objective optimization

Find an approximate second-order stationary point of the full objective:

\textbf{Status.} Bounds missing

\textbf{TASK tags.} formulation: Second order stationarity; task family: Single objective

\textbf{MODEL tags.} convexity: Convexity not assumed; geometry: Full space; smoothness: Kth derivative lipschitz

\textbf{ORACLE tags.} access order: Higher-order interface; feedback quality: Exact; interface family: Exact jet k; operation: Exact jet k; public information: Hidden objects explicitly declared; public information: Known upper bound; public information: Known exact value; public information: Public inputs explicitly declared

\textbf{ALGORITHMS tags.} adaptivity: Adaptive; randomization: Deterministic algorithms; randomization: Private randomness allowed; restriction: No additional span restriction explicitly imposed

\textbf{OUTPUT tags.} certificate: No additional output certificate required; feasibility: Required; object: Point; postprocessing: Unqueried output explicitly allowed

\textbf{METRIC tags.} criterion: Second order stationarity; criterion: Stationarity measure

\textbf{GUARANTEE tags.} aggregation: Per instance; mode: Deterministic; mode: Probability; randomness: Algorithm private seed

\textbf{RESOURCE tags.} budget: Fixed worst-case budget; measure: Oracle calls; precision: Bit precision not counted

\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{1. Setting specification}
\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Task}
Find an approximate second-order stationary point of the full objective:


\AtlasMath{\|\nabla f(\widehat{x})\|_2\le\varepsilon_g,\qquad\nabla^2f(\widehat{x})\succeq-\varepsilon_H I_d.}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Admissible model}
The objective \AtlasInlineMath{f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}} is \AtlasInlineMath{C^k} and bounded below; nonconvexity is allowed.

The objective has a finite infimum, and the public initial point \AtlasInlineMath{x_0} satisfies \AtlasInlineMath{f(x_0)-\inf_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\le\Delta}.


\AtlasMath{\|D^{k}f(x)-D^{k}f(y)\|_{\mathrm{op},2}\le M_k\|x-y\|_{2}.}


Fix \AtlasInlineMath{k\ge2}; no additional lower-order regularity bound is imposed.

Admissible parameter domain:


\AtlasMath{d\ge1,\quad k\ge2;\quad\text{all other parameters satisfy their tabulated ranges}.}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Oracle interface}
Each query selects \AtlasInlineMath{x} in \AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d} and returns the complete exact tuple \AtlasInlineMath{J_{k}f(x)=(f(x),Df(x),\ldots,D^{k}f(x))}. The fixed objective uniquely determines the response, with no stochastic noise.

The public inputs are \AtlasInlineMath{x_0}, the target accuracy, and \AtlasInlineMath{d}, \AtlasInlineMath{k}, \AtlasInlineMath{\Delta}, \AtlasInlineMath{M_k}, \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_g}, \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_H}. Numerical constants are admissible bounds and need not equal the sharp constants of the instance. The objective, unqueried derivatives, minimizer and minimum value are hidden.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Output}
Return \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{x}\in \mathbb{R}^d}.

The output may be an unqueried point, a feasible average of past iterates, or another feasible postprocessing result. No function value or additional computable certificate is required.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Loss or accuracy criterion}
The base error is


\AtlasMath{\mathcal{E}(\widehat{x})=\max\left\{\frac{\|\nabla f(\widehat{x})\|_2}{\varepsilon_g},\frac{[-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(\widehat{x}))]_+}{\varepsilon_H}\right\}.}


\AtlasInlineMath{[a]_+=\max\{a,0\}}, and \AtlasInlineMath{\lambda_{\min}} denotes the smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix. The target is \AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{E}(\widehat{x})\le1}, where \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_g} and \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_H} are independent positive tolerances.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Resource accounting}
Each primitive response specified under ORACLE costs one unit. Queries at new points introduced by any inner procedure also count toward the total.

The resource budget is a fixed worst-case cap on every execution path. Initialization, stopping checks, and all actual responses in a batch are included.

Arithmetic, linear algebra, tensor operations, storage, and global solution of known models are free. Bit complexity, communication, and wall-clock time are not counted.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Algorithm views and success guarantees}
\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Deterministic}
Arbitrary measurable adaptive deterministic algorithms are allowed.

No linear-span, Krylov or zero-respecting restriction is imposed. Memory and internal computation are unrestricted.

Information is acquired adaptively in query order. Parallel submission does not reduce the number of actual responses counted. There is no communication-round or memory budget. Exact real arithmetic and arbitrarily small positive query separations are allowed.

Choose one algorithm from the public inputs, then require its guarantee separately for every admissible instance and oracle law.


\AtlasMath{\max\left\{\frac{\|\nabla f(\widehat{x})\|_2}{\varepsilon_g},\frac{[-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(\widehat{x}))]_+}{\varepsilon_H}\right\}\le 1.}


The running-cost guarantee is specified separately under RESOURCE.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Randomized}
Arbitrary measurable adaptive algorithms with private randomness are allowed.

No linear-span, Krylov or zero-respecting restriction is imposed. Memory and internal computation are unrestricted.

Information is acquired adaptively in query order. Parallel submission does not reduce the number of actual responses counted. There is no communication-round or memory budget. Exact real arithmetic and arbitrarily small positive query separations are allowed.

Choose one algorithm from the public inputs, then require its guarantee separately for every admissible instance and oracle law.


\AtlasMath{\Pr\!\left[\max\left\{\frac{\|\nabla f(\widehat{x})\|_2}{\varepsilon_g},\frac{[-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(\widehat{x}))]_+}{\varepsilon_H}\right\}\le 1\right]\ge\frac23.}


Expectation or probability is evaluated after fixing the instance; randomness comes from the algorithm's private random seed.

The running-cost guarantee is specified separately under RESOURCE.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{2. Notation and parameters}
\AtlasInlineMath{x,\widehat{x},x_0}: Query or decision point, algorithm output, and public initial point. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d}: Real coordinate space; vectors use the Euclidean norm unless otherwise stated. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d} is a positive integer.

\AtlasInlineMath{\langle u,v\rangle,\ \|u\|_2}: Euclidean inner product and norm.


\AtlasMath{\langle u,v\rangle=u^\top v,\qquad\|u\|_2=\sqrt{\langle u,u\rangle}.}


\AtlasInlineMath{D^jf(x),\ \nabla f(x),\ \nabla^2f(x)}: Fréchet derivative of order \AtlasInlineMath{j}, gradient and Hessian. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{j\in\{0,\ldots,k\}} and \AtlasInlineMath{D^0f=f}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}},\ \|T\|_{\mathrm{op},2}}: Induced operator norm of a Euclidean multilinear tensor; the spectral norm for matrices.


\AtlasMath{\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|T\|_{\mathrm{op},2}=\sup_{\|u_1\|_2,\ldots,\|u_j\|_2\le1}|T[u_1,\ldots,u_j]|.}


\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{E}}: Base error defined in the metric specification; expectation or probability aggregation is imposed by the guarantee.

\AtlasInlineMath{N}: Total number of original oracle calls; the unit cost is specified in the resource convention. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{N\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{T^*}: Minimum worst-case budget for one algorithm to meet the requirement on the full instance class, within the specified regime, guarantee and resource projection. Expected-resource specifications instead minimize the per-instance expected budget.

\AtlasInlineMath{O,\Omega,\Theta,\widetilde{O}}: Asymptotic upper bounds, lower bounds, matching bounds up to constants, and upper bounds omitting the declared logarithmic factors. \textbf{Domain:} Hidden constants, fixed parameters, and omitted logarithmic variables are specified for each bound.

\AtlasInlineMath{\inf,\sup,\min,\max}: Infimum, supremum, attained minimum and attained maximum.

\AtlasInlineMath{c,C}: Positive universal constants without assigned numerical values; a subscript permits dependence only on the indicated fixed parameters. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<c,C<\infty}.

\AtlasInlineMath{J_{k}f(x)}: Function value and the complete tuple of derivatives from order one through the specified maximum order.


\AtlasMath{J_{k}f(x)=(f(x),Df(x),\ldots,D^{k}f(x)).}


\AtlasInlineMath{f,f^*}: Unknown objective and its global infimum over the specified feasible domain.


\AtlasMath{f^*=\inf_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}f(x).}


\AtlasInlineMath{\lambda_{\min}(A),[z]_+}: The smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix and the positive part of a scalar.


\AtlasMath{[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}.}


\AtlasInlineMath{I_d}: The identity matrix in dimension \AtlasInlineMath{d}.

\AtlasInlineMath{d}: Ambient dimension; dimension requirements are stated separately for each bound. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{d\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{k}: Maximum order of the query interface and Taylor model; this integer is fixed before other parameters are compared. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge2}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\Delta}: Upper bound on the difference between the objective value at the known initial point and its global infimum. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\Delta\ge0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{M_k}: Global Lipschitz upper bound for the order-\AtlasInlineMath{k} derivative in the tensor operator norm. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{M_k\ge0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_g}: Gradient-norm tolerance \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_g>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_H}: Tolerance for negative Hessian curvature \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon_H>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{C_k}: A sufficiently large positive constant depending only on the fixed order \AtlasInlineMath{k}, without a numerical value specified. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{C_k>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{A}: Gradient workload \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{A\ge0}.


\AtlasMath{A=\Delta\,(M_k)^{\frac{1}{k}}\,((\varepsilon_g)^{(-1)\,(\frac{k+1}{k})}).}


\AtlasInlineMath{B}: Negative-curvature workload \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{B\ge0}.


\AtlasMath{B=\Delta\,((M_k)^{\frac{2}{k-(1)}})\,((\varepsilon_H)^{(-1)\,(\frac{k+1}{k-(1)})}).}


\AtlasInlineMath{C_0}: Fixed gradient-dominance ratio in this regime, retained as a symbolic constant. \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{C_0>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{E},\Pr}: Expectation and probability after fixing the instance; their randomness sources are specified by the guarantee.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{B1 - High-order regularized models jointly control the next-point gradient and smallest eigenvalue}
\textbf{Admission.} Included in the bracket

\textbf{Direction.} upper

\textbf{View.} Deterministic

\textbf{Witness or lower-bound scope.} Deterministic witness

\AtlasMath{C_k(1+A+B)}
\textbf{Sources.} \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.04044}{[3]}

\textbf{Conditions.} \AtlasInlineMath{d\ge 1,\Delta>0,M_k>0,\varepsilon_g>0,\varepsilon_H>0}

\textbf{Oracle correspondence.} Each query selects \AtlasInlineMath{x} in \AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d} and returns the complete exact tuple \AtlasInlineMath{J_{k}f(x)=(f(x),Df(x),\ldots,D^{k}f(x))}. The fixed objective uniquely determines the response, with no stochastic noise.

\textbf{Guarantee conversion.} Deterministic-error guarantee for every instance

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Native field: body}
Native pointer: /proofs/0/body; canonical SHA-256: 8b2356c60fae01a303ef034de840ae671bb7c46284ad3aff7534fc86c1242ca8

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy The noiseless specialization in ACDFSS20,\allowbreak{} Appendix H.2,\allowbreak{} gives a zero-respecting curvature lower bound\newline{}\$\$\textbackslash{}Omega\_\allowbreak{}k\textbackslash{}left(\textbackslash{}frac\textbackslash{}Delta\{\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H\}\textbackslash{}min\_\allowbreak{}\{2\textbackslash{}le j\textbackslash{}le k\}(M\_\allowbreak{}j/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H)\textasciicircum{}\{2/\allowbreak{}(j-1)\}\textbackslash{}right),\allowbreak{}\$\$\newline{}within the nonautomatic window \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H\textbackslash{}le c\_\allowbreak{}kM\_\allowbreak{}1\$. For deterministic algorithms,\allowbreak{} adaptively rotate the smooth gated chain. Unactivated gates have every derivative zero,\allowbreak{} so each complete jet reveals at most the next direction,\allowbreak{} including its value response. Choose later directions orthogonal to prior queries and,\allowbreak{} at the end,\allowbreak{} to the unqueried output. A sufficient dimension \$C\_\allowbreak{}k(1+N)\$ accommodates all constraints. Determinism ensures that the final single rotated instance produces the constructed transcript. This seed-dependent adversary argument does not prove an arbitrary-randomized lower bound.\newline{}\newline{}With only \$M\_\allowbreak{}k\$ controlled,\allowbreak{} choose width \$b\textbackslash{}asymp(\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H/\allowbreak{}M\_\allowbreak{}k)\textasciicircum{}\{1/\allowbreak{}(k-1)\}\$ and amplitude \$a\textbackslash{}asymp\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}Hb\textasciicircum{}2\$. Then\newline{}\$\$N\textbackslash{}asymp\_\allowbreak{}k\textbackslash{}Delta M\_\allowbreak{}k\textasciicircum{}\{2/\allowbreak{}(k-1)\}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H\textasciicircum{}\{-(k+1)/\allowbreak{}(k-1)\}.\$\$\newline{}Additional \$\textbackslash{}beta\$-smoothness requires \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H\textbackslash{}le c\textbackslash{}beta\$. Combine this hard family with the separate gradient hard family by taking their maximum,\allowbreak{} which is equivalent up to a factor two to the sum;\allowbreak{} no one instance is claimed to realize both difficulties simultaneously.\newline{}\newline{}For arbitrary randomized exact second-order algorithms,\allowbreak{} REUSE26v2's deterministic-loss subclass supplies the separate curvature result. Its gated chain has \$O(N)\$ value range and dimension-independent Hessian and third-derivative operator bounds. With \$\textbackslash{}gamma=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H\$,\allowbreak{} spatial scale of order \$\textbackslash{}gamma\$,\allowbreak{} and amplitude of order \$\textbackslash{}gamma\textasciicircum{}3\$,\allowbreak{} take N of order \$\textbackslash{}gamma\textasciicircum{}\{-3\}\$. A radial cutoff and wall at radius of order \$\textbackslash{}gamma\textasciicircum{}\{-1\}\$ prevent unrestricted distant queries or outputs from bypassing the chain:\allowbreak{} outside the hard region the gradient is too large,\allowbreak{} while the transition region retains negative curvature. Conditional exposure of hidden rotation directions and concentration over every query and the final output give the sufficient dimension\newline{}\$\$d\textbackslash{}ge C\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}theta[1+\textbackslash{}gamma\textasciicircum{}\{-4\}\textbackslash{}log(2+\textbackslash{}gamma\textasciicircum{}\{-1\})+\textbackslash{}gamma\textasciicircum{}\{-3\}],\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}qquad\textbackslash{}theta=\allowbreak{}(\textbackslash{}beta,\allowbreak{}M\_\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}Delta).\$\$\newline{}Thus,\allowbreak{} for fixed positive \$\textbackslash{}theta\$ and sufficiently small independent tolerances,\allowbreak{} the primary result yields \$\textbackslash{}Omega\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}theta\}(\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H\textasciicircum{}\{-3\})\$. Combining it with the randomized gradient lower bound gives the linked exact-J2 bracket. Constants may depend on fixed \$\textbackslash{}theta\$;\allowbreak{} this is not a joint-parameter lower bound with universal constants,\allowbreak{} nor a higher-order randomized theorem.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy For each fixed j,\allowbreak{} use the jth-order regularized method,\allowbreak{} reading only the relevant part of the complete k-jet. Its budget is \$C\_\allowbreak{}j[1+\textbackslash{}Delta M\_\allowbreak{}j\textasciicircum{}\{1/\allowbreak{}j\}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}\{-(j+1)/\allowbreak{}j\}]\$. All parameters are public,\allowbreak{} so an algorithm may select the smallest proved budget. This minimum is an envelope of complete algorithms.\newline{}\newline{}For the lower bound,\allowbreak{} use the robust CDHS smooth chain \$h\_\allowbreak{}N\$,\allowbreak{} whose initial gap is at most \$C\_\allowbreak{}kN\$,\allowbreak{} whose gradient stays bounded away from zero before completion,\allowbreak{} and whose jth-derivative Lipschitz modulus is at most a constant \$\textbackslash{}ell\_\allowbreak{}j\$ depending only on j. Set \$f(x)=\allowbreak{}a h\_\allowbreak{}N(x/\allowbreak{}b)\$ with\newline{}\$\$a/\allowbreak{}b=\allowbreak{}K\_\allowbreak{}k\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g,\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}qquad\newline{}b=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}max\_\allowbreak{}\{1\textbackslash{}le j\textbackslash{}le k\}(K\_\allowbreak{}k\textbackslash{}ell\_\allowbreak{}j\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g/\allowbreak{}M\_\allowbreak{}j)\textasciicircum{}\{1/\allowbreak{}j\}.\$\$\newline{}Then \$\textbackslash{}operatorname\{Lip\}(D\textasciicircum{}jf)=\allowbreak{}a\textbackslash{}ell\_\allowbreak{}j/\allowbreak{}b\textasciicircum{}\{j+1\}\textbackslash{}le M\_\allowbreak{}j\$ for every j simultaneously. Choosing N proportional to \$\textbackslash{}Delta/\allowbreak{}a\$ gives N of order A. For A above a fixed k-dependent threshold,\allowbreak{} deterministic resisting rotations fit in \$d\textbackslash{}ge C\_\allowbreak{}k(1+A)\$;\allowbreak{} the classical randomized radial construction fits in \$d\textbackslash{}ge C\_\allowbreak{}k(1+A)\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(3+A)\$. These are sufficient dimensions.\newline{}\newline{}If the primary result is stated as time to query a successful point,\allowbreak{} append one complete-jet query at the algorithm's final output. A lower bound of N then gives an original-budget lower bound N-1,\allowbreak{} of the same order in the nontrivial A region. This handles arbitrary unqueried outputs without changing the success quantifier.\newline{}\newline{}For \$k=\allowbreak{}2\$,\allowbreak{} the common scaling gives \$A=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}Delta\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}\{-2\},\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}sqrt\{M\_\allowbreak{}2\}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}\{-3/\allowbreak{}2\}\textbackslash{}\}\$. Keep the zero-query region \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}ge2\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta\$ separate;\allowbreak{} the whole domain is not uniformly Theta(1+A). Dimension improvements proved for a highest-order-only model do not automatically preserve all lower-order budgets.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy At x,\allowbreak{} form \$m\_\allowbreak{}x(s)=\allowbreak{}T\_\allowbreak{}k(f;\allowbreak{}x,\allowbreak{}s)+a\_\allowbreak{}kM\_\allowbreak{}k\textbackslash{}|s\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}\{k+1\}\$,\allowbreak{} choosing \$a\_\allowbreak{}k\$ sufficiently large,\allowbreak{} depending only on k,\allowbreak{} to dominate the Taylor remainder with slack. For \$M\_\allowbreak{}k>0\$ the model is coercive,\allowbreak{} so it has a global minimizer,\allowbreak{} available under the declared free internal computation. Comparing the model at s and zero and applying the value remainder gives\newline{}\$\$f(x)-f(x+s)\textbackslash{}ge c\_\allowbreak{}kM\_\allowbreak{}k\textbackslash{}|s\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}\{k+1\}.\$\$\newline{}Model first-order optimality and the gradient remainder give\newline{}\$\$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x+s)\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le C\_\allowbreak{}kM\_\allowbreak{}k\textbackslash{}|s\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}k.\$\$\newline{}If the next point is not \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\$-stationary,\allowbreak{} the decrease is at least \$c\_\allowbreak{}kM\_\allowbreak{}k\textasciicircum{}\{-1/\allowbreak{}k\}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}\{(k+1)/\allowbreak{}k\}\$. The total decrease is at most \$\textbackslash{}Delta\$,\allowbreak{} so after the displayed number of calls,\allowbreak{} including initialization and final verification,\allowbreak{} stationarity is reached.\newline{}\newline{}This is the parameter restoration of the regularized-model argument in BGMST17,\allowbreak{} Lemmas 2.1{\AtlasUnicodeText –}\allowbreak{}2.3 and Theorem 2.5. Its normalization is \$(k-1)!L=\allowbreak{}M\_\allowbreak{}k\$. Separate function and derivative evaluations in the source cost only a fixed multiple when complete jets are charged as one. The argument is about information calls and does not assert an inexpensive arithmetic implementation of global nonconvex model minimization.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy For a full-space differentiable objective with \$f(x\_\allowbreak{}0)-\textbackslash{}inf f\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}Delta\$,\allowbreak{} the condition \$\textbackslash{}Delta=\allowbreak{}0\$ makes \$x\_\allowbreak{}0\$ a global minimizer. Its gradient is zero,\allowbreak{} and its Hessian is positive semidefinite whenever it exists. Thus first-order and spectral second-order stationarity require no query. An objective-gap target also requires no query when \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}f\textbackslash{}ge\textbackslash{}Delta\$. Nonnegative query cost proves exact optimality of these zero bounds.\newline{}\newline{}If a public gradient-Lipschitz bound \$\textbackslash{}beta\$ is part of the specification,\allowbreak{} the descent lemma gives \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x\_\allowbreak{}0)\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}le2\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta\$. For convex full-space objectives with a minimizer within distance \$R\$,\allowbreak{} it also gives \$f(x\_\allowbreak{}0)-f\textasciicircum{}*\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}beta R\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\$ and \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x\_\allowbreak{}0)\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}beta R\$. These sufficient zero-query regions require that explicit first-order regularity assumption. If only the highest derivative is controlled,\allowbreak{} positive quadratics can have arbitrary curvature and arbitrarily large initial gap despite zero highest-order modulus.\newline{}\newline{}On a connected Euclidean domain,\allowbreak{} \$M\_\allowbreak{}k=\allowbreak{}0\$ or \$M\_\allowbreak{}\{k,\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}nu\}=\allowbreak{}0\$ makes \$D\textasciicircum{}kf\$ constant,\allowbreak{} so \$f\$ is a polynomial of degree at most \$k\$. One complete jet determines all coefficients. Under the specified free internal computation,\allowbreak{} a known polynomial can then be optimized on a compact public domain,\allowbreak{} or combined with a public regularizer and solved through the declared known-model interface.\newline{}\newline{}A bounded-below polynomial on the full space need not attain its infimum. For approximate spectral stationarity,\allowbreak{} shift \$x\_\allowbreak{}0\$ to zero and minimize \$f(x)+\textbackslash{}eta\textbackslash{}|x\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\$. This function is coercive,\allowbreak{} and its minimizer \$x\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}eta\$ satisfies \$\textbackslash{}eta\textbackslash{}|x\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}eta\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}Delta\$,\allowbreak{} \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}eta)\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}sqrt\{2\textbackslash{}eta\textbackslash{}Delta\}\$,\allowbreak{} and \$\textbackslash{}nabla\textasciicircum{}2f(x\_\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}eta)\textbackslash{}succeq-\textbackslash{}eta I\$. Choosing \$\textbackslash{}eta\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}H,\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(2\textbackslash{}Delta)\textbackslash{}\}\$ meets both targets. For global objective accuracy,\allowbreak{} exact polynomial coefficients permit arbitrary-accuracy internal global optimization;\allowbreak{} no additional unknown-function query is needed.\newline{}\newline{}To exclude zero queries in a nontrivial region,\allowbreak{} choose two positive quadratics centered on opposite sides of \$x\_\allowbreak{}0\$,\allowbreak{} with the same public budgets and disjoint acceptable-output sets. A zero-query algorithm has the same output distribution on both instances,\allowbreak{} so their success probabilities sum to at most one. It cannot succeed with probability at least \$2/\allowbreak{}3\$ on each. With only highest-order regularity,\allowbreak{} curvature can be increased until the acceptable sets are disjoint at any prescribed positive accuracy and positive localization radius. In an initial-gap model with additional curvature restrictions,\allowbreak{} retain the bound's explicit accuracy and compatibility window.\newline{}\newline{}If both a global PL constant \$\textbackslash{}mu\$ and a gradient-Lipschitz upper bound \$\textbackslash{}beta\$ are supplied,\allowbreak{} then \$2\textbackslash{}mu(f-f\_\allowbreak{}*)\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}le2\textbackslash{}beta(f-f\_\allowbreak{}*)\$. When \$\textbackslash{}mu>\textbackslash{}beta>0\$,\allowbreak{} every gap is zero and the class contains only constant objectives. This degeneracy does not apply without the extra \$\textbackslash{}beta\$ assumption.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy Retain the frozen full-space C\textasciicircum{}k,\allowbreak{} bounded-below objective,\allowbreak{} gap,\allowbreak{} jet,\allowbreak{} output and free-known-model contracts and HO\_\allowbreak{}ENDPOINTS. M\_\allowbreak{}k=\allowbreak{}0 makes D\textasciicircum{}k f constant,\allowbreak{} so the Taylor polynomial of degree at most k recovered from J\_\allowbreak{}k f(x0) equals f everywhere. After this single query set eta=\allowbreak{}min(epsilon\_\allowbreak{}H,\allowbreak{}epsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(2Delta))>0 and globally minimize the known coercive polynomial f(x)+eta||x-x0||\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2 using the permitted free model solution. At a minimizer y,\allowbreak{} eta||y-x0||\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2<=\allowbreak{}f(x0)-inf f<=\allowbreak{}Delta;\allowbreak{} therefore ||grad f(y)||=\allowbreak{}eta||y-x0||<=\allowbreak{}sqrt(2eta Delta)<=\allowbreak{}epsilon\_\allowbreak{}g and Hess f(y)>=\allowbreak{}-eta I>=\allowbreak{}-epsilon\_\allowbreak{}H I. No further oracle check is required and y may be unqueried. This does not assume that f attains its own infimum. For the lower bound fix lambda>epsilon\_\allowbreak{}g\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(2Delta),\allowbreak{} a=\allowbreak{}sqrt(2Delta/\allowbreak{}lambda),\allowbreak{} and f\_\allowbreak{}+(x)=\allowbreak{}lambda||x-x0-a e1||\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{} f\_\allowbreak{}-(x)=\allowbreak{}lambda||x-x0+a e1||\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2. Both have gap Delta and Lipschitz D\textasciicircum{}k modulus zero for every k>=\allowbreak{}2. Their Hessians are positive definite;\allowbreak{} their acceptable outputs are disjoint balls of radius epsilon\_\allowbreak{}g/\allowbreak{}lambda because a>epsilon\_\allowbreak{}g/\allowbreak{}lambda. A zero-query output law is the same on both instances,\allowbreak{} so its two success probabilities sum to at most one. It cannot give probability >=\allowbreak{}2/\allowbreak{}3 on each;\allowbreak{} the deterministic case follows as well. Integer query counts give cost>=\allowbreak{}1. Thus the upper and lower costs are exactly one,\allowbreak{} uniformly in dimension and both tolerances. At Delta=\allowbreak{}0 the retained zero-query branch applies instead.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy Read arXiv:\allowbreak{}2609.28202v2,\allowbreak{} Definition 3.1 and Theorems 3.2 and 3.4,\allowbreak{} PDF pp.5-6,\allowbreak{} archived characters 13323-16400,\allowbreak{} source SHA256 5129c1f6b8ae94f321c0541890578a5ef396ec08583340160ed877699bae11f9. Set n=\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{} p=\allowbreak{}k,\allowbreak{} L\_\allowbreak{}p=\allowbreak{}M\_\allowbreak{}k,\allowbreak{} epsilon=\allowbreak{}epsilon\_\allowbreak{}g. Then the complete component p-jet is precisely one target complete jet and S\_\allowbreak{}p=\allowbreak{}1+A. The source class is bounded below with initial gap at most Delta and Lipschitz D\textasciicircum{}k bound M\_\allowbreak{}k,\allowbreak{} with no lower-order regularity budget. Any algorithm meeting the target simultaneous gradient/\allowbreak{}Hessian condition with probability at least 2/\allowbreak{}3 also meets its gradient condition with that probability,\allowbreak{} for every positive epsilon\_\allowbreak{}H. The source lower bound is therefore necessary for the target. Theorem 3.4 supplies hard dimension at most C\_\allowbreak{}k(1+A)log(3+A);\allowbreak{} choose the k-only source constant sufficiently large. For an ambient dimension above this value,\allowbreak{} pad a hard function h(z) by f(z,\allowbreak{}w)=\allowbreak{}h(z). Projection of every query gives an exact equal-cost source query;\allowbreak{} all derivatives involving dummy coordinates vanish and the remaining complete jet agrees with h. Project the arbitrary output as well. Gap,\allowbreak{} lower boundedness,\allowbreak{} tensor operator Lipschitz bound,\allowbreak{} fixed-path cost and success probability are preserved. Hence an ambient target algorithm below c\_\allowbreak{}k(1+A) would contradict the source theorem. We adopt the conservative A>=\allowbreak{}C\_\allowbreak{}k subregion. No relation between B and A is used. This is a new q2 bound,\allowbreak{} not a relabeling or merger of the old q1 bound.\par\endgroup
